## Goals for this week

(a) Make "signal" and "system" precise.

(b) Understand linearity.

(c) How to measure the size of a signal: energy &amp; power.

(d) How to measure the angle between signals.

(e) Useful signals: Dirac delta and friends.

## Signals as vectors

We've seen signals &amp; systems through examples. In this lecture, we'll develop a language to
represent these things mathematically.  At first this may seem quite abstract, but it ends up being extremely powerful, as we'll see throughout the semester.

We will build on what we know from linear algebra.

A square matrix $A$ maps a vector to another vector of the same dimension:

$$
\underset{\textstyle \mathbb{R}^{n}}{y} \;=\;
\underset{\textstyle \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}}{A}\;
\underset{\textstyle \mathbb{R}^{n}}{u}
$$

If $n = 2$, we can visualise $A$ in the plane as <u>scaling</u>, <u>rotating</u>, skewing and
reflecting $u$ to produce $y$:


We measure the scaling using a <u>norm</u>:

$$ \|u\| \;=\; \sqrt{u \cdot u} \;=\; \sqrt{u_1^{2} + u_2^{2}}. $$

We measure the rotation using the <u>dot product</u>:

$$ \cos\theta \;=\; \frac{u \cdot y}{\|u\|\,\|y\|}. $$

**How do we extend these ideas to signals?**

Given a continuous signal, we can approximate one period as an infinite dimensional
vector.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
```{=html}
<div id="w-sample" class="widget"></div>
```
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
![Sampling a continuous signal at spacing $\Delta$: as $\Delta \to 0$, the sum
$\sum_t u_t y_t\,\Delta$ becomes the integral $\langle u, y\rangle$.](figs/w-sample.png){#fig-sample width=100%}
:::

$$ \dots\; x_{-1}\;\; x_{0}\;\; x_{1}\;\; x_{2}\;\; x_{3}\;\; x_{4}\;\; x_{5}\;\; x_{6}\;\; x_{7}\; \dots $$

The dot product between these vectors is

$$ \sum_{t=-\infty}^{\infty} u_t\, y_t \;=\; u \cdot y $$

If we let the sampling become <u>infinitesimally fine</u>, we integrate over the samples,
and have an <u>inner product</u>:

$$ \langle u, y\rangle \;:=\; \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} u(t)\,y(t)\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

For complex signals, we add a complex conjugate:

$$ \boxed{\;\langle u, y\rangle \;:=\; \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} u(t)\,\overline{y}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\;} $$

<!-- CHECK: the handwritten page conjugates the FIRST slot, ∫ ū(t) y(t) dt, but then
     lists ⟨αu,y⟩ = α⟨u,y⟩ and ⟨u,βy⟩ = β̄⟨u,y⟩ — which is the conjugate-second-slot
     convention. The two can't both hold. Per your instruction I've moved the bar onto
     the second slot so the definition and the four properties below agree. Everything
     downstream (E(u) = ⟨u,u⟩, ⟨·,·⟩_P) is unaffected, since |u|² = u ū either way. -->

Some useful properties of the inner product:

1. $\langle u_1 + u_2,\, y\rangle \;=\; \langle u_1, y\rangle + \langle u_2, y\rangle$
2. $\langle \alpha u,\, y\rangle \;=\; \alpha\,\langle u, y\rangle$
3. $\langle u,\, \beta y\rangle \;=\; \overline{\beta}\,\langle u, y\rangle$
4. $\langle u, y\rangle \;=\; \overline{\langle y, u\rangle}$

So the inner product is linear in its first argument and conjugate-linear in its second.

## The size of a signal: energy &amp; power

We can use the inner product to measure the size of a signal:

$$ \boxed{\;E(u) \;=\; \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |u(t)|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\;} $$

This is the <u>signal energy</u>. The complex conjugate in $\langle u, y\rangle$
guarantees $E(u)$ is real.

**Example:**

$$
u(t) = \begin{cases} e^{-t}, & t \geq 0 \\[2pt] 0, & t < 0. \end{cases}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
E(u) &= \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-2t}\,\mathrm{d}t \\[4pt]
     &= \left. \frac{-1}{2}\, e^{-2t} \right|_{0}^{\infty} \\[4pt]
     &= \frac{1}{2}\, e^{0} \;=\; \frac{1}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

What if $u(t) = A\cos(\omega t)$?

$$ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} A^{2}\cos^{2}(\omega t)\,\mathrm{d}t \;=\; \infty \;\dots $$

Take the average power:

::: {.note}
$\text{energy} = \displaystyle\int \text{power}\;\mathrm{d}t$
:::

$$ \boxed{\;P(u) \;=\; \lim_{W \to \infty} \frac{1}{2W} \int_{-W}^{W} |u(t)|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t.\;} $$

If $u(t) = u(t + T)$ for some $T$,
each period contributes the same, so we get the average.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{W \to \infty} \frac{1}{2W} \int_{-W}^{W} |u(t)|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t
&= \lim_{k \to \infty} \frac{1}{2kT}\left( \cdots
   \underbrace{\int_{-kT}^{-(k-1)T} |u(t)|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t}_{\textstyle =\int_{0}^{T}|u(t)|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t}
   + \underbrace{\int_{-(k-1)T}^{-(k-2)T} |u(t)|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t}_{\textstyle =\int_{0}^{T}|u(t)|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t}
   + \cdots + \int_{-T}^{0} |u(t)|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t + \cdots
   + \int_{(k-1)T}^{kT} |u(t)|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t \right) \\[10pt]
&= \lim_{k \to \infty} \frac{1}{2k} \cdot 2k \cdot \frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^{T} |u(t)|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t \\[6pt]
&= \boxed{\;P(u) = \frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^{T} |u(t)|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t.\;}
\end{aligned}
$$

This is the average power of a periodic signal.

**Example:** what is the power of $u(t) = A\cos(\omega t)$

$$ \text{Period} = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} $$

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(u) &= \frac{\omega}{2\pi} \int_{0}^{\frac{2\pi}{\omega}} A^{2}\cos(\omega t)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t \\[6pt]
     &= \frac{\omega}{2\pi} \int_{0}^{\frac{2\pi}{\omega}} A^{2}\,\frac{1 + \cos(2\omega t)}{2}\,\mathrm{d}t \\[6pt]
     &= \frac{\omega}{2\pi} \left[ A^{2}\,\frac{t}{2} \;+\; A^{2}\,\frac{\sin(2\omega t)}{4\omega} \right]_{0}^{\frac{2\pi}{\omega}} \\[6pt]
     &= \frac{\omega}{2\pi} \left( A^{2}\,\frac{\frac{2\pi}{\omega}}{2}
        \;+\; A^{2}\,\frac{\overset{\textstyle 0}{\overbrace{\sin\!\left(\tfrac{4\pi}{\omega}\,\omega\right)}}}{4\omega} \right) \\[6pt]
     &= \frac{A^{2}}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Example:** what is the power of
$u(t) = \begin{cases} e^{-t}, & t \geq 0 \\[2pt] 0, & t < 0 \end{cases}$ ?

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(u) &= \lim_{W \to \infty} \frac{1}{2W} \int_{-W}^{W} |u(t)|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t \\[6pt]
     &= \lim_{W \to \infty} \frac{1}{2W} \int_{0}^{W} e^{-2t}\,\mathrm{d}t \\[6pt]
     &= \lim_{W \to \infty} \frac{1}{2W} \left[ \frac{-1}{2}\,e^{-2t} \right]_{0}^{W} \\[6pt]
     &= \lim_{W \to \infty} \underbrace{\frac{1}{2W}}_{\textstyle \to 0}
        \left[ \underbrace{\frac{1}{2}\,e^{0}}_{\textstyle \frac{1}{2}}
        \;-\; \underbrace{\frac{1}{2}\,e^{-2W}}_{\textstyle \to 0} \right] \\[6pt]
     &= 0.
\end{aligned}
$$

```{=html}
<hr style="border:0;border-top:1.5px solid #00468C;margin:1.6em 0;">
```

Through the last two examples, we have discovered two types of signals:

<u>Power signals</u>: infinite energy, finite power. $\qquad \cos(\omega t)$

<u>Energy signals</u>: finite energy, zero power. $\qquad e^{-t}$

For periodic signals, we can also define the <u>rms</u> (root mean square):

$$ \boxed{\;u_{\mathrm{RMS}} \;=\; \sqrt{P(u)}\;} $$

It turns out $P$ comes from a different inner product, which is finite for power signals,

$$ \langle u, y\rangle_{P} \;:=\; \frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^{T} u(t)\, \overline{y}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

We then have

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(u) &= \langle u, u\rangle_{P}, \\[4pt]
u_{\mathrm{RMS}} &= \sqrt{\langle u, u\rangle_{P}} \;=\; \|u\|_{P}.
\end{aligned}
$$

**Example:** the RMS of mains power in Australia is 230 V. What is the
peak voltage?

$$ v(t) = V_p \cos(\omega t), \qquad \omega = 2\pi \cdot 50 = 100\pi \;\text{rad/s},
   \qquad T = \tfrac{1}{50} = 20\ \text{ms}. $$

From the earlier example, $P(v) = \dfrac{V_p^{2}}{2}$, so

$$ v_{\mathrm{RMS}} \;=\; \sqrt{P(v)} \;=\; \frac{V_p}{\sqrt{2}}
   \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad V_p \;=\; 230\sqrt{2} \;=\; 325\ \text{V}. $$

Why do we use $v_{\mathrm{RMS}}$ as the nominal voltage? Let's calculate the power
delivered to a nominal resistive load $R$, such as a kettle.

Instantaneous power is

$$ p(t) \;=\; v(t)\, i(t) \;=\; \frac{v(t)^{2}}{R} \;=\; \frac{V_p^{2}}{R}\cos^{2}(\omega t). $$

Average over one period:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_{\mathrm{avg}} &= \frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^{T} \frac{|v(t)|^{2}}{R}\,\mathrm{d}t
   \;=\; \frac{1}{R}\, P(v) \\[6pt]
&= \frac{V_p^{2}}{2R} \\[6pt]
&= \frac{v_{\mathrm{RMS}}^{2}}{R}.
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.note}
$P(v)$ is a *signal* power, so its units are $\mathrm{V}^{2}$ — not joules. Dividing by
$R$ turns it into a physical power in watts.
:::

This says that $v_{\mathrm{RMS}}$ is the equivalent <u>DC voltage</u> that delivers the
same power across a nominal load.

For $R = 23\,\Omega$,

$$ P_{\mathrm{avg}} = \frac{230^{2}}{23} = 2300\ \text{W}, \qquad
   i_{\mathrm{RMS}} = \frac{230}{23} = 10\ \text{A}. $$

## The angle between two signals

We can use this inner product to measure the angle between two signals using
$\cos\theta = \dfrac{\langle u, y\rangle_{P}}{\|u\|_{P}\,\|y\|_{P}}$

$$ x_1(t) = 3\cos\omega t, \qquad x_2(t) = 4\cos\!\left(\omega t + \frac{\pi}{4}\right) $$

$$ \langle x_1(t), x_2(t)\rangle_{P} \;=\; \frac{\omega}{2\pi} \int_{0}^{\frac{2\pi}{\omega}}
   12\cos(\omega t)\cos\!\left(\omega t + \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\mathrm{d}t $$

Plug through to get $\;6\cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$.

$$ \|x_1\|_{P} = \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}, \qquad \|x_2\|_{P} = \frac{4}{\sqrt{2}} \qquad
   \text{using the previous example.} $$

So

$$ \cos\theta \;=\; \frac{6\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)}{6}, \qquad \theta = \frac{\pi}{4}. $$

::: {.note}
The angle between two sinusoids is their phase shift.
:::

## Linear systems, gain and delay

Back to our starting point, that a conformal matrix <u>scales</u> &amp; <u>rotates</u> vectors.

A <u>linear system</u> performs these same operations on <u>signals</u>.

For example, a <u>static gain</u> scales a signal:

```{=html}
<div style="text-align:center">
<svg viewBox="0 0 300 80" width="280" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"
     aria-label="Block diagram: input u into a block labelled k, output ku.">
  <defs>
    <marker id="ahB" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7"
            orient="auto-start-reverse">
      <path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="#00468C"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <text x="24" y="45" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" fill="#00468C" font-style="italic">u</text>
  <line x1="40" y1="40" x2="120" y2="40" stroke="#00468C" stroke-width="1.2" marker-end="url(#ahB)"/>
  <rect x="122" y="20" width="52" height="40" fill="none" stroke="#00468C" stroke-width="1.2"/>
  <text x="142" y="46" font-family="Arial" font-size="15" fill="#00468C" font-style="italic">k</text>
  <line x1="174" y1="40" x2="250" y2="40" stroke="#00468C" stroke-width="1.2" marker-end="url(#ahB)"/>
  <text x="258" y="45" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" fill="#00468C" font-style="italic">ku</text>
</svg>
</div>
```

If $u = \cos(\omega t)$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
(ku)_{\mathrm{RMS}} &= \sqrt{P(ku)} \\[4pt]
                    &= \frac{k}{\sqrt{2}} \qquad \text{from the previous example.}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$ u_{\mathrm{RMS}} \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}. $$

The <u>gain</u> of the system is

$$ \frac{(ku)_{\mathrm{RMS}}}{u_{\mathrm{RMS}}} \;=\; k. $$

What type of system rotates signals, that is, imparts phase lag?

The pure delay,

```{=html}
<div style="text-align:center">
<svg viewBox="0 0 300 80" width="280" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"
     aria-label="Block diagram: input u into a block labelled D tau, output y.">
  <defs>
    <marker id="ahB2" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7"
            orient="auto-start-reverse">
      <path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="#00468C"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <text x="24" y="45" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" fill="#00468C" font-style="italic">u</text>
  <line x1="40" y1="40" x2="118" y2="40" stroke="#00468C" stroke-width="1.2" marker-end="url(#ahB2)"/>
  <rect x="120" y="20" width="56" height="40" fill="none" stroke="#00468C" stroke-width="1.2"/>
  <text x="134" y="46" font-family="Arial" font-size="15" fill="#00468C" font-style="italic">D</text>
  <text x="146" y="51" font-family="Arial" font-size="11" fill="#00468C" font-style="italic">&#964;</text>
  <line x1="176" y1="40" x2="250" y2="40" stroke="#00468C" stroke-width="1.2" marker-end="url(#ahB2)"/>
  <text x="258" y="45" font-family="Arial" font-size="14" fill="#00468C" font-style="italic">y</text>
</svg>
</div>
```

$$ y(t) = u(t - \tau). $$

E.g. if $u(t) = \cos(\omega t)$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
y(t) &= \cos\big(\omega(t - \tau)\big) \\[2pt]
     &= \cos(\omega t - \omega\tau).
\end{aligned}
$$

From the previous example,

$$ \cos\theta \;=\; \cos(-\omega\tau) \;=\; \cos(\omega\tau) $$

$$ \underline{\;\theta = \omega\tau.\;} $$

The pure delay gives a phase shift of $\omega\tau$, and gain $\underline{1}$.

Pure delay and static gain are two simple examples of <u>linear, time-invariant</u> (LTI)
systems. We will see many more next week!

## Linearity and time invariance

What do linear and time invariant mean?

Linear =

homogeneous (scale invariant): $\;A(\alpha u) = \alpha A(u)$.

and additive: $\;A(u_1 + u_2) = A(u_1) + A(u_2)$. $\qquad$ *Add inputs $\to$ add outputs.*

Together, we have <u>superposition</u>: $\;A(\alpha u_1 + \beta u_2) = \alpha A(u_1) + \beta A(u_2)$.

Time invariant: behaviour doesn't depend on starting time:

$$ A(D_\tau u) = D_\tau A(u) \quad \text{for all } \tau. \qquad \text{\small shift input} \to \text{\small shift output.} $$

**Quick quiz:** which maps from $u$ to $y$ are linear?

**Example:** check the delay is linear:

$$
\begin{aligned}
D_\tau(\alpha u) &= \alpha\, u(t - \tau) = \alpha\, D_\tau(u)
   &&\Longrightarrow\; \text{homogeneous.} \\[6pt]
D_\tau(u_1 + u_2) &= u_1(t - \tau) + u_2(t - \tau) = D_\tau(u_1) + D_\tau(u_2)
   &&\Longrightarrow\; \text{additive.}
\end{aligned}
$$

Is it time invariant?

$$ D_\tau\big(D_\mu u\big) \;=\; D_\tau\big(u(t - \mu)\big) \;=\; u(t - \mu - \tau)
   \;=\; D_\mu\big(D_\tau(u)\big) \;\checkmark $$

## Now: some useful signals

We have already seen the most used signal in this course: $u(t) = e^{st}$,
$s \in \mathbb{C}$, and all its components: $e^{-t}$, $e^{t}$, $\sin t$, $\cos t$.

Now we'll introduce three more signals which we will see many more times.

### ① Dirac delta

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
```{=html}
<div id="w-delta" class="widget"></div>
```
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
![The triangle $u_\varepsilon(t)$ of base $\varepsilon$ and height $2/\varepsilon$,
area 1, narrowing towards the Dirac delta as $\varepsilon \to 0$.](figs/w-delta.png){#fig-delta width=80%}
:::

$u_\varepsilon(t)$ is the triangle of base $\varepsilon$ and height $\tfrac{2}{\varepsilon}$, so

$$ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} u_\varepsilon(t)\,\mathrm{d}t
   \;=\; \frac{1}{2}\,\varepsilon\,\frac{2}{\varepsilon}
   \;=\; \varepsilon\,\frac{1}{\varepsilon} \;=\; 1. $$

The Dirac delta, or impulse, $\delta(t)$, may be defined as

$$ \boxed{\;\delta(t) \;=\; \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} u_\varepsilon(t)\;} $$

```{=html}
<div style="text-align:center">
<svg viewBox="0 0 260 130" width="240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"
     aria-label="The Dirac delta drawn as a single upward arrow at the origin.">
  <defs>
    <marker id="ahD" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7"
            orient="auto-start-reverse">
      <path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="#00468C"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <line x1="20" y1="100" x2="240" y2="100" stroke="#00468C" stroke-width="1.2"
        marker-end="url(#ahD)"/>
  <text x="246" y="105" font-family="Arial" font-size="13" fill="#00468C" font-style="italic">t</text>
  <line x1="90" y1="100" x2="90" y2="25" stroke="#00468C" stroke-width="1.6"
        marker-end="url(#ahD)"/>
</svg>
</div>
```

infinite height, area 1.

The Dirac delta has an extremely important property: <u>the sifting property</u>.

Let $y(t)$ be an arbitrary continuous signal. Then

$$ \boxed{\;\langle y, \delta\rangle \;=\; \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y(t)\,\bar \delta(t)\,\mathrm{d}t
   \;=\; y(0)\;} $$

**Sketch of proof:**

If $\varepsilon$ is small, $y(t) \simeq y(0)$ on $[0, \varepsilon]$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(t)\, y(t)\,\mathrm{d}t
  &= \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \int_{0}^{\varepsilon} u_\varepsilon(t)\, y(t)\,\mathrm{d}t \\[6pt]
  &\simeq y(0) \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \int_{0}^{\varepsilon} u_\varepsilon(t)\,\mathrm{d}t \\[6pt]
  &= y(0).
\end{aligned}
$$

(Can be made precise using a continuity argument).

What about $\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(t - \tau)\, y(t)\,\mathrm{d}t$ ?

Let $\sigma = t - \tau$. $\;\mathrm{d}t = \mathrm{d}\sigma$.

Then we have

$$ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(\sigma)\, y(\sigma + \tau)\,\mathrm{d}\sigma \;=\; y(\tau). $$

$$ \boxed{\;\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(t - \tau)\, y(t)\,\mathrm{d}t \;=\; y(\tau)\;}
   \qquad \text{\small the sifting property.} $$

::: {.note}
**NOTE:** The above definition of the Dirac delta is not unique. It can be defined in
many ways, for example using different limits, measures or distributions. The important
thing (which really defines it) is the sifting property.
:::

::: {.note}
**NOTE:** A Dirac delta only really makes sense inside an integral, so it represents an
<u>area</u> of 1, rather than a height.
:::

#### The scaling property

What is $\delta(\alpha t)$?

$$ \delta(\alpha t) \;=\; \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} u_\varepsilon(\alpha t). $$

```{=html}
<div style="text-align:center">
<svg viewBox="0 0 560 300" width="540" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"
     aria-label="The triangle u epsilon of alpha t, drawn against the alpha-t axis for
                 alpha positive and for alpha negative, and then against the t axis where
                 its base is epsilon over alpha and its area is one over the modulus of alpha.">
  <defs>
    <marker id="ahS" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7"
            orient="auto-start-reverse">
      <path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="#00468C"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>

  <!-- alpha > 0 : decreasing triangle on 0..epsilon of the (alpha t) axis -->
  <line x1="30" y1="100" x2="215" y2="100" stroke="#00468C" stroke-width="1.2" marker-end="url(#ahS)"/>
  <text x="220" y="105" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#00468C" font-style="italic">&#945;t</text>
  <path d="M 70 100 L 70 30 L 130 100" stroke="#00468C" fill="none" stroke-width="1.6"/>
  <text x="62" y="115" font-family="Arial" font-size="11" fill="#00468C">0</text>
  <text x="125" y="115" font-family="Arial" font-size="11" fill="#00468C">&#949;</text>
  <line x1="152" y1="100" x2="152" y2="32" stroke="#00468C" stroke-width="1"
        marker-start="url(#ahS)" marker-end="url(#ahS)"/>
  <text x="158" y="70" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#00468C">2/&#949;</text>
  <text x="40" y="26" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#00468C" font-style="italic">u&#949;(&#945;t)</text>
  <text x="245" y="70" font-family="Arial" font-size="13" fill="#00468C">&#945; &gt; 0</text>

  <!-- alpha < 0 : mirrored -->
  <line x1="215" y1="240" x2="30" y2="240" stroke="#00468C" stroke-width="1.2" marker-end="url(#ahS)"/>
  <text x="24" y="256" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#00468C" font-style="italic">&#945;t</text>
  <path d="M 175 240 L 175 170 L 115 240" stroke="#00468C" fill="none" stroke-width="1.6"/>
  <text x="178" y="255" font-family="Arial" font-size="11" fill="#00468C">0</text>
  <text x="110" y="255" font-family="Arial" font-size="11" fill="#00468C">&#949;</text>
  <line x1="196" y1="240" x2="196" y2="172" stroke="#00468C" stroke-width="1"
        marker-start="url(#ahS)" marker-end="url(#ahS)"/>
  <text x="202" y="210" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#00468C">2/&#949;</text>
  <text x="112" y="166" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#00468C" font-style="italic">u&#949;(&#945;t)</text>
  <text x="245" y="210" font-family="Arial" font-size="13" fill="#00468C">&#945; &lt; 0</text>

  <!-- the same triangle read on the t axis -->
  <line x1="520" y1="180" x2="340" y2="180" stroke="#00468C" stroke-width="1.2" marker-end="url(#ahS)"/>
  <text x="334" y="196" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#00468C" font-style="italic">t</text>
  <path d="M 480 180 L 480 105 L 415 180" stroke="#00468C" fill="none" stroke-width="1.6"/>
  <line x1="500" y1="180" x2="500" y2="107" stroke="#00468C" stroke-width="1"
        marker-start="url(#ahS)" marker-end="url(#ahS)"/>
  <text x="506" y="146" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#00468C">2/&#949;</text>
  <text x="400" y="200" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#00468C">&#949;/&#945;</text>
  <text x="330" y="120" font-family="Arial" font-size="13" fill="#00468C">area 1/|&#945;|</text>
</svg>
</div>
```

Let $\sigma = \alpha t$. Then $\sigma = \varepsilon \;\Rightarrow\; t = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{\alpha}$,
so on the $t$ axis the triangle has base $\left|\dfrac{\varepsilon}{\alpha}\right|$ and height
$\dfrac{2}{\varepsilon}$, giving

$$ \text{area} \;=\; \frac{1}{2}\left|\frac{\varepsilon}{\alpha}\right|\frac{2}{\varepsilon}
   \;=\; \frac{1}{|\alpha|}. $$

The limit is therefore an impulse of area $\dfrac{1}{|\alpha|}$ at the origin:

$$ \boxed{\;\delta(\alpha t) \;=\; \frac{1}{|\alpha|}\,\delta(t)\;} $$

#### Example: radar

Radar systems emit a pulse train and measure its reflection to find the distance to
objects. We can model this as a sequence of deltas.

```{=html}
<div style="text-align:center">
<svg viewBox="0 0 420 150" width="400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"
     aria-label="A radar dish at the left, an outgoing and a returning ray to an aircraft
                 at the right, and the range r marked between them.">
  <defs>
    <marker id="ahR" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7"
            orient="auto-start-reverse">
      <path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="#00468C"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <!-- radar dish: parabolic reflector opening to the right, feed at the focus,
       back-mounted mast on a tripod base -->
  <path d="M 40 4 Q 4 36 40 68" stroke="#00468C" fill="none" stroke-width="1.8"/>
  <line x1="22" y1="36" x2="40" y2="36" stroke="#00468C" stroke-width="1.2"/>
  <circle cx="40" cy="36" r="3" fill="#00468C"/>
  <line x1="22" y1="36" x2="14" y2="36" stroke="#00468C" stroke-width="1.4"/>
  <line x1="14" y1="36" x2="14" y2="100" stroke="#00468C" stroke-width="1.4"/>
  <path d="M 3 108 L 14 100 L 25 108" stroke="#00468C" fill="none" stroke-width="1.4"/>
  <line x1="0" y1="108" x2="28" y2="108" stroke="#00468C" stroke-width="1.2"/>
  <!-- aircraft: fuselage, swept wings, tail -->
  <path d="M 296 34 L 366 34 L 380 30 L 366 26 L 296 26 Z" stroke="#00468C" fill="none" stroke-width="1.4"/>
  <path d="M 336 26 L 318 8 L 344 26" stroke="#00468C" fill="none" stroke-width="1.4"/>
  <path d="M 336 34 L 318 52 L 344 34" stroke="#00468C" fill="none" stroke-width="1.4"/>
  <path d="M 300 26 L 292 12 L 308 26" stroke="#00468C" fill="none" stroke-width="1.4"/>
  <!-- out and back -->
  <line x1="48" y1="20" x2="286" y2="20" stroke="#00468C" stroke-width="1.2" marker-end="url(#ahR)"/>
  <line x1="286" y1="52" x2="48" y2="52" stroke="#00468C" stroke-width="1.2" marker-end="url(#ahR)"/>
  <!-- range -->
  <line x1="14" y1="124" x2="336" y2="124" stroke="#00468C" stroke-width="1"
        marker-start="url(#ahR)" marker-end="url(#ahR)"/>
  <text x="172" y="143" font-family="Arial" font-size="13" fill="#00468C" font-style="italic">r</text>
</svg>
</div>
```

Total path length: $2r$. Round trip time: $\dfrac{2r}{c} = t_d$. So

$$ r \;=\; \frac{c\,t_d}{2}. $$

Delay $\Rightarrow$ distance. E.g. a $1\,\mu\text{s}$ delay gives

$$ r = \tfrac{1}{2}\,(3\times10^{8})(10^{-6}) = 150\ \text{m}. $$

If there are $N$ targets at ranges $r_i$ with reflectivities $a_i$, the reflected signal is

$$ y(t) \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{N} a_i\, \delta\!\left(t - \frac{2 r_i}{c}\right). $$

**Unambiguous range.** Suppose we transmit radar pulses at a frequency
$f = \dfrac{1}{T}$:

```{=html}
<div style="text-align:center">
<svg viewBox="0 0 340 110" width="320" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"
     aria-label="A train of four impulses spaced T apart along the time axis.">
  <defs>
    <marker id="ahT" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7"
            orient="auto-start-reverse">
      <path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="#00468C"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <line x1="20" y1="70" x2="320" y2="70" stroke="#00468C" stroke-width="1.4"/>
  <g stroke="#00468C" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#ahT)">
    <line x1="60" y1="70" x2="60" y2="22"/>
    <line x1="130" y1="70" x2="130" y2="22"/>
    <line x1="200" y1="70" x2="200" y2="22"/>
    <line x1="270" y1="70" x2="270" y2="22"/>
  </g>
  <line x1="60" y1="92" x2="130" y2="92" stroke="#00468C" stroke-width="1"
        marker-start="url(#ahT)" marker-end="url(#ahT)"/>
  <text x="90" y="107" font-family="Arial" font-size="12" fill="#00468C" font-style="italic">T</text>
</svg>
</div>
```

Suppose we measure an echo at time $t_d$ since the most recent pulse. Which pulse is it
an echo of? The distance could be

$$ \frac{c\,t_d}{2}, \qquad \frac{c\,(t_d + T)}{2}, \qquad \frac{c\,(t_d + 2T)}{2},
   \qquad \dots $$

The range is only known up to

$$ R_u \;=\; \frac{cT}{2}, $$

the <u>unambiguous range</u>.

Higher $T$: larger range, but slower updates.

How to deal with this? Transmit at two frequencies — the range has to be consistent with
both measurements.

```{=html}
<hr style="border:0;border-top:1.5px solid #00468C;margin:1.6em 0;">
```

### ② The unit step

Another important function is the <u>unit step</u> or <u>Heaviside</u> function:

$$
\begin{aligned}
H(t) &:= \int_{-\infty}^{t} \delta(\varsigma)\,\mathrm{d}\varsigma \\[6pt]
     &= \begin{cases} 0, & t < 0 \\[2pt] 1, & t \geq 0. \end{cases}
\end{aligned}
$$

### ③ The pulse

Finally, the pulse function $p_\tau(t)$:

$$
p_\tau(t) := \begin{cases} 1, & -\dfrac{\tau}{2} \leq t \leq \dfrac{\tau}{2} \\[6pt]
0, & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}
$$
